blocks.text: 1. PDF Parsing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708358-164976946.png
PDF Parsing, covering another common document ingestion source with its own challenges, moves from web pages to a different, widespread file format.
It extracts real, usable text out of a widespread but tricky file format.
2. Recapping The Preview
Web Crawling's closing recap previewed PDF parsing as another common ingestion source with its own challenges, briefly described there.
This topic gives that preview its complete, dedicated treatment, exploring every detail only briefly hinted at before.
3. Recapping Extracting Content From HTML
Web Crawling covered extracting content from HTML: HTML stores content with explicit tags marking structure.
PDF instead stores content as positioned visual elements, with no such explicit structure.
4. Why PDFs Are Tricky To Parse

blocks.alt: Why PDFs Are Tricky To Parse
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708358-342302332.png
A PDF records where each character sits on a page, not which words form a sentence.
Reconstructing real paragraphs and reading order requires careful inference, which is the core difficulty this topic explores.

blocks.text: 5. Text-Based Versus Scanned PDFs
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708579-841157993.png
A text-based PDF still contains real, extractable character data underneath its own layout.
A scanned PDF instead contains only a flat image, with no text data at all, a crucial distinction.
6. Preview Of OCR For Scanned PDFs

blocks.alt: Preview Of OCR For Scanned PDFs
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708580-250393957.png
Optical character recognition, covered generally in OCR, recovers text from those flat, scanned images.
Without OCR, a scanned PDF contributes zero usable text to the document collection.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: OCR is the necessary bridge between a scanned PDF's own flat image and any actually usable text for the ingestion pipeline.

blocks.text: 7. Preserving Tables And Layout
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708580-169271199.png
Tables present a particular challenge, since their own row and column structure is purely visual.
A naive parser can scramble table content into a meaningless jumble of words, a real, common failure mode.
8. Multi-Column Layout Challenges
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708581-555060493.png
Multi-column documents risk having text extracted in the wrong reading order.
Sentences from separate columns can get mixed together into one garbled, incoherent paragraph, another common failure mode.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing Which PDF Parsing Approach Fits A Given Document

blocks.alt: Recognizing Which PDF Parsing Approach Fits A Given Document
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708581-81284844.png
Direct text extraction suits text-based PDFs with clean, real character data.
OCR becomes necessary for scanned, image-only PDFs.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates reconstructing reading order from position-based text fragments, similar to raw PDF extraction output.

code.content:
positioned_fragments = [
    {"text": "results.", "x": 300, "y": 100},
    {"text": "The quarterly", "x": 50, "y": 100},
    {"text": "revenue grew", "x": 150, "y": 100},
]

def reconstruct_reading_order(fragments):
    sorted_fragments = sorted(fragments, key=lambda f: (f["y"], f["x"]))
    return " ".join(f["text"] for f in sorted_fragments)

print(f"Raw positioned fragments: {positioned_fragments}")
reconstructed = reconstruct_reading_order(positioned_fragments)
print(f"\nReconstructed text, sorted by position: '{reconstructed}'")

print("\nNote: this simple x-then-y sort breaks down for real multi-column layouts,")
print("where a naive sort by position alone mixes text from separate columns")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows text fragments reordered by their own recorded position into a coherent sentence, while noting where that simple approach breaks down.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming every PDF contains extractable text without checking whether it is actually scanned.
Extracting table content without preserving its own row and column structure.
Applying a simple top-to-bottom text sort to multi-column documents, scrambling the reading order.
Skipping OCR entirely for scanned PDFs, losing all of that document's own content.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: PDF parsing extracts real, usable text out of a widespread but tricky file format.
HTML stores content with explicit structural tags; PDF stores positioned visual elements instead.
A PDF records where each character sits on a page, not which words form a sentence.
Text-based PDFs contain extractable character data; scanned PDFs contain only a flat image.
OCR is the necessary bridge for recovering text from scanned, image-only PDFs.
Tables present a particular challenge, since their row and column structure is purely visual.
Multi-column layouts risk extracting text in the wrong reading order, mixing separate columns.
Direct extraction suits text-based PDFs; OCR becomes necessary for scanned, image-only PDFs.
